title: Comparison and Talent.
transcript: Life imitates chess. If you look at a bishop, you might think that it's much better than a knight. It can move across the entire board in an [music] instant. And in an open position like this one, it can start picking up the pawns like flies. So, if we were to take this position in a vacuum, we might [music] come to the conclusion that the bishop is much better than the knight. But if we take this same position and we start adding a bunch of extra pawns, all of a sudden, we will find that the bishop has no targets. And as a matter of fact, it's pretty much rendered useless. While the knight's jumping abilities will allow him to get inside the position and start attacking all of the opponent's weaknesses. But you would never know that if you only ever played [music] open positions. You would learn that the bishop is just objectively better >> [music] >> and you would convince yourself of that. But at the end of the day, it is all about the environment of the pieces. They thrive in different [music] positions. And when we take all of this into consideration, we find out that actually the knight and the bishop are worth about the same. And it is going to be up to the player to move these pieces in a way that [music] uses their full potential.
